svg.title: One policy clause becomes three control objectives, and several technical means whose costs differ by an order of magnitude
svg.desc: The clause "customer data may not leave the country" translates into three verifiable control objectives: storage location constrained, only de-identified aggregates cross the border, and access paths auditable. Each objective can be met by several technical means. The same clause can be satisfied by an encrypted virtual leased line, by application-layer encryption, or by a physically dedicated circuit, and the cost of those three differs by roughly an order of magnitude.
svg.text: From a sentence in a contract to a device configuration
Policy speaks in obligations; design speaks in constraints. The translation is the designer's work, and it is where cost is decided
policy clause — natural language, not testable
"Customer personal data must not leave the country."
one sentence, and three departments will read it three ways
translate
control objectives — verifiable statements
storage location is constrained to in-country facilities,
only de-identified aggregates may cross the border,
every access path to the data is auditable.
each one can be tested; "must not leave" cannot
select
technical means — replaceable, and priced
in-country isolated zone: VRF or overlay separation
one-way de-identified egress with an approval record
central policy plane: configuration only, no data; local logs
SAME CLAUSE, THREE PRICE POINTS
"Any traffic crossing networks we do not own must be encrypted" — three ways to satisfy it:
encrypted VLL over existing dark fibre
IPsec or MACsec on a circuit you already lease; changes one configuration
reuses the plant, so the cost is a licence and a weekend of work
application-layer encryption
TLS end to end, so the network stays plain and the application carries the burden
no circuit change, but every integration must be touched and re-tested
physically dedicated circuit, no sharing
a separate fibre pair or wavelength per customer, encrypted or not
satisfies the clause most convincingly and costs the most, every month
The designer's job is to lay out these three with their prices, not to jump
to the most expensive one — and not to let procurement choose in the dark.
A clause answers "what must be true". A control objective answers "how would we test it". A technical means answers "what do we configure".
Skipping the middle step is why designs get challenged in audit: nothing links the configuration back to the sentence it was meant to satisfy.
